title: White Trash: The 400-Year Untold History of Class in America
author: Nancy Isenberg
target_audience: General readers interested in U.S. history
Students and scholars of sociology, history, and American studies
Individuals interested in social class, race, and inequality
Readers curious about American identity and cultural politics
core_themes: The persistent reality and consequences of class in American society
The myth of an American classless society
The origins and evolution of poor white identity
The intersection of class, race, and American politics
primary_purpose: To challenge the prevailing narrative of classlessness in American society by tracing the history and stigmatization of poor whites over four centuries, showing how class divisions have shaped, and continue to shape, American identity and democracy.

structure_format.narrative_style: Analytical, historical, and highly-researched with a critical tone
structure_format.organization: Chronological, divided into sections and chapters that trace class from colonial America to the present
features: Analysis of cultural texts, political speeches, and media

key_concepts_lessons: Class has been a defining—though often denied—element in American life since the colonial era.
Labels like 'crackers,' 'squatters,' 'rednecks,' and 'white trash' have been used to delineate and stigmatize poor whites.
The American dream of meritocracy has historically excluded large segments of the white population.
Class boundaries were reinforced through law, land policy, and social shaming.
Political and cultural treatment of poor whites reflects deeper anxieties about race, democracy, and privilege.
Contemporary political and social realities continue to be shaped by this class history.
notable_features: Sweeping, 400-year historical scope from Jamestown to the 21st century
Challenges foundational myths about American society
Meticulous research drawing from politics, literature, and popular culture
Exploration of social, legal, and economic mechanisms for perpetuating class
cultural_historical_context: Published in 2016, amid intense national conversations about race, class, and the political power of the white working class, the book responds to both renewed scholarly interest in social inequality and immediate events in American politics.
reception_impact: Critically acclaimed for its scope and insight, appearing on bestseller lists and receiving award nominations
Praised for shedding light on a frequently ignored aspect of U.S. history
Influential in shaping contemporary debates about the white working class and American identity
Some critics note a heavy focus on white poverty at the expense of broader intersectional analysis
comparable_titles: Deer Hunting with Jesus by Joe Bageant
The Sum of Us by Heather McGhee
Democracy in Chains by Nancy MacLean
